records.rationale: Correct sum-to-product derivation and the doubled peak rate of the absolute envelope, yielding the difference-frequency beat law.

evidence.title: OpenStax, University Physics 1: Beats
evidence.finding: Sum-to-product yields an amplitude envelope; adjacent amplitude maxima give the beat rate equal to the absolute difference of cyclic frequencies.
The signed cosine envelope has angular rate |omega1-omega2|/2. Its absolute peaks repeat at beat angular rate |omega1-omega2|, corresponding to cyclic rate |f1-f2|=|omega1-omega2|/(2pi).
The first omega expression is an angular frequency, while the final f expression is in Hz; their numerical values are not interchangeable without 2pi.

records.rationale: The U(1) description is correct, but the matrix generalization has an extra factor of i. Exp(A) is unitary for skew-Hermitian A; exp(iA) is unitary for Hermitian A.

evidence.title: Bader et al., Exponential of skew-Hermitian matrices
evidence.finding: The matrix exponential of a skew-Hermitian generator is unitary. In the physics convention exp(iH), H is Hermitian rather than skew-Hermitian.

records.rationale: Multipath interference is a valid fading mechanism, but the given cos² law requires an equal-amplitude coherent two-path model. Generic multipath amplitudes and additional paths need not follow that formula.

evidence.finding: Two coherent components with real amplitudes A1,A2 have power proportional to A1²+A2²+2*A1*A2*cos(delta_phi). A normalized cos²(delta_phi/2) law is the equal-amplitude two-path special case.
With A1=2 and A2=1, power is 5+4cos(delta_phi), ranging from 1 to 9, not a normalized cos² law that reaches zero.
This hold does not deny that interference explains some driving-related radio fading.
